title: Undo an edit without losing the one next to it
summary: Throw away one file's changes, unstage another, and pull a third back from an old commit — using git restore, the command that replaced the overloaded git checkout.
mental_model: `restore` answers 'make this file look like X'. Default X is the index; `--staged` makes the index look like HEAD; `--source=<commit>` makes it look like any commit you name. One verb, one target, no surprises.
danger: `git restore <file>` discards working-tree edits permanently. They were never committed, so no reflog and no recovery. This is the one genuinely destructive command in everyday git.

steps.title: Read the two-column status carefully
steps.why: sensor.py is staged, pump.py is not. The left column is the index, the right column is the working tree. Every restore decision starts by reading which column the letter is in.

steps.title: Unstage sensor.py without losing the edit
steps.why: `--staged` copies HEAD's version into the index only. The working tree is untouched, so your edit survives — it is simply no longer scheduled for the next commit.
steps.expect: sensor.py moves to the right-hand column and still says kelvin.

steps.title: Throw away the broken pump edit
steps.why: This is the destructive one. `restore` with no flags overwrites the working-tree file from the index — which here matches HEAD. The 9999 and the BROKEN flag are gone for good.

verify.label: pump.py is back to its committed state

steps.title: Recover an old version of a file
steps.why: `--source` reaches into any commit. Here we pull schedule.py as it existed one commit ago — useful when a change turns out to be wrong but you do not want to revert the whole commit.
steps.expect: LIGHTS_ON back to 08:00, showing as a working-tree modification.

steps.title: Restore into the index and the working tree at once
steps.why: `--staged --worktree` together set both. This is the closest thing to 'make this file exactly like that commit, ready to commit' in one step.
steps.expect: schedule.py back to 07:30 and the tree clean of it.

steps.title: Why restore exists at all
steps.why: `git checkout` did branch switching, file restoring and commit inspection with the same word — the single biggest source of git confusion. `switch` and `restore` split it in two. Old tutorials still show checkout; both work.

verify.label: the broken pump edit was discarded
the sensor edit was unstaged but kept
verify.hint: git restore --staged sensor.py — without --staged you would have destroyed it

verify.label: schedule.py was put back to its committed state after the experiment

pitfalls: `git restore <file>` on uncommitted work is unrecoverable. If you are unsure, `git stash` instead — it is reversible.
`git restore --staged` unstages; `git reset <file>` does the same thing. restore is the clearer spelling.
`git restore .` from a subdirectory only restores that subdirectory. Use `:/` for the whole repo.
`git checkout -- <file>` is the old spelling of the destructive form. Same danger, worse name.
cheatsheet: pull one file from any commit
